title: Depth-cued change blindness
summary: A flicker change-blindness task (Rensink, O'Regan & Clark, 1997) in which the cue names a depth plane instead of a place or an object. The main set uses 48 photograph pairs of real-looking places with two separate depths, a near layer within arm's reach of the camera and a far layer 10 to 30 m away; each place was photographed twice, once with the change on a near object and once on a far object. A word, NEAR or FAR, names the plane of the change on 75% of trials; a fixation target on the gray field starts every search at the centre; then A A A' A' flicker until SPACE, and a keyed report of where and what. Drawn two-plane scenes with switchable monocular depth cues remain as separate sets. The measure is alternations to identification on valid against invalid trials, for each plane.
references: Rensink, R. A., O'Regan, J. K., & Clark, J. J. (1997). To see or not to see: The need for attention to perceive changes in scenes. Psychological Science, 8(5), 368-373. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9280.1997.tb00427.x
Posner, M. I. (1980). Orienting of attention. Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology, 32(1), 3-25. https://doi.org/10.1080/00335558008248231
Downing, C. J., & Pinker, S. (1985). The spatial structure of visual attention. In M. I. Posner & O. S. M. Marin (Eds.), Attention and Performance XI (pp. 171-187). Erlbaum.

Atchley, P., Kramer, A. F., Andersen, G. J., & Theeuwes, J. (1997). Spatial cuing in a stereoscopic display: Evidence for a 'depth-aware' attentional focus. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 4(4), 524-529. https://doi.org/10.3758/BF03214343

Ghirardelli, T. G., & Folk, C. L. (1996). Spatial cuing in a stereoscopic display: Evidence for a "depth-blind" attentional spotlight. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 3(1), 81-86. https://doi.org/10.3758/BF03210744
He, Z. J., & Nakayama, K. (1995). Visual attention to surfaces in three-dimensional space. PNAS, 92(24), 11155-11159. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.92.24.11155

Thaler, L., Schütz, A. C., Goodale, M. A., & Gegenfurtner, K. R. (2013). What is the best fixation target? The effect of target shape on stability of fixational eye movements. Vision Research, 76, 31-42. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.visres.2012.10.012
Atkinson Hyperlegible typeface, Braille Institute of America (SIL Open Font License 1.1).

tasks.title: Depth-cued flicker change detection
tasks.summary: Cue word NEAR or FAR 3 s, gray field with a central fixation target 1 s, then A A A' A' flicker (240 ms images, 80 ms blanks) until SPACE (max 60 s), then where (box 1-4) and what kind (arrow keys).

deviations.original: Experiment 3: a word naming the changing object (p. 370)
deviations.here: a word naming the depth plane of the change: NEAR or FAR
deviations.reason: the question of this experiment: does attention to a depth plane, rather than to an object or a place, speed change detection

deviations.here: 75% valid, 25% invalid (main set); a set adds neutral NEAR OR FAR trials
deviations.reason: invalid trials are needed to measure what the cue buys; neutral trials split it into benefit and cost

deviations.here: 48 generated photographs of real-looking places (27 places, each photographed with a near and a far change; 6 more for practice), composited so A and A' differ only at the change
deviations.reason: the paper's photographs are not available, and the changed object's plane has to be controlled: each place has one change on each plane

deviations.here: generated two-plane displays: 8 near and 8 far shapes, two of each per quadrant, 3 far shapes partly occluded; depth from monocular cues only (relative size, occlusion, cast shadows, blur, aerial perspective, texture); one new scene per trial, drawn from its seed
deviations.reason: the planes must be interleaved over the picture so that a depth cue is not a spatial cue, and the changed object's plane must be controlled

deviations.here: not manipulated; the change is on the near or the far plane, within the same 3-11 dva eccentricity band on both
deviations.reason: plane of the change is the factor here; eccentricity is matched instead

deviations.here: keyed: one of four boxes (two on near objects, two on far ones), then the kind of change with an arrow key
deviations.reason: no experimenter needed to score; equal boxes per plane so the report does not reveal the plane

deviations.here: 96 trials (2 planes x 3 change types x 16), each scene once
deviations.reason: enough invalid trials (24) for a within-subject cue effect per plane

deviations.here: 2.0 dva: drawn scenes toward the most open space, photographs toward the vertical midline
deviations.reason: keeps moved objects clear of their neighbours and inside the picture

deviations.here: Thaler et al.'s (2013) ABC target on the 1-s gray field; free viewing during the flicker
deviations.reason: every search starts at the centre, from where the changes' eccentricity is matched across planes
